newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS -Producers to revoke arabica quotas, up sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -Producers to revoke arabica quotas, up sale.

text.p: The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) agreed on Thursday to relax its export curbs in the first half of 1997 in support of arabica coffee growers after the recent surge in world prices.
The group, at a technical meeting in London, decided to lift arabica exports by 500,000 60-kg bags but left robusta quotas intact.
The meeting was called by key Central American arabica producers which had sought to raise the supply of arabica coffee to the market.
Central American delegates welcomed the plan. "There has been a lot of pressure on us from our growers," said a Costa Rican delegate.
The decision also reflected producer concerns about runaway arabica coffee prices and the impact on consumption, and the growing margins between arabicas and robustas.

Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said in Paris on Thursday that leading producers should raise sales quotas or anticipate a part of their quota for later in the year in order to put downward pressure on prices.
He said prices must remain above $1.30-$1.40 a lb if the world wants good-quality coffee. A level above $2.00 is considered excessive and $1.00 to $1.10 is insufficient to assure quality.
Arabica prices have started to come down lately after rising by more than 50 percent since early this year on a combination of factors including the recent truck drivers' strike in Colombia.
Prices hit a peak of $2.09 on the New York arabica futures in early March. It closed at 169.15 cents on Thursday.
Under the latest ACPC plan, which is subject to the council approval, members will release an additional 200,000 bags of arabica coffee to the market, ACPC President Rubens Barbosa of Brazil said.
It also agreed to revoke a previous decision to reduce exports of arabica by 300,000 bags during the same period.

The ACPC decided at a meeting in Rio de Janeiro in January to cut 1.3 million bags of exports -- 1.0 million bags of robusta and 300,000 bags of arabica. So the net effect of Thursday's decision will be a reduction of 800,000 bags of exports, Barbosa added.
The 1.3 million bag cut agreed in January would have bring exports by the 14-member group down to 24.98 million in the first six months of 1997.

But the technical group -- comprising Brazil, Indonesia, Colombia, Ivory Coast, Uganda and El Salvador -- kept the robusta quotas unchanged at 1.0 million bags. Representatives from Honduras, Costa Rica and Kenya also attended the one-day meeting.
The ACPC supply news drew a mixed reaction from analysts.
Lawrence Eagles, head of research at brokerage GNI, said the producer decision was seen as positive.
"The group is concerned by the high prices of arabica coffee and the continued weakeness of robusta in relation to arabica," he said.
"But the market yawned at the news. It showed that most of the pricing for that extra coffee could have been done," he said.
Judith Ganes, an analyst at Merrill Lynch said the news did not come as a surprise as producers had been wanting to stabilise the market by trying to release more coffee.
The market will absorb the additional quantity and that's still probably not enough to satisfy demand, she added.
Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka viewed the news as bearish.
"The chances of the market moving higher is now diminished," he said.
The ACPC full council is expected to ratify Thursday's decision by the technical committee at a meeting in May in London.
Barbosa said the committee did not discuss the quota distribution among the arabica producer members.
He also said the technical group would start discussions from next month on new market mechanism to succeed the current one-year export programme which expires this June.
((--London Newsroom 44 171 542-4985))
